From Admission to Invariants:
Measuring Deviation in Delegated Agent Systems

Marcelo Fernandez Affiliation: TraslaIA Email: info@traslaia.com
Abstract

Autonomous agent systems are governed by enforcement mechanisms that flag hard constraint violations at runtime. The Agent Control Protocol [3] identifies a structural limit of such systems (§17): a correctly-functioning enforcement engine can enter a regime in which behavioral drift is invisible to it, because the enforcement signal operates below the layer where deviation is measurable. We show that enforcement-based governance is structurally unable to determine whether an agent’s behavior remains within the admissible behavior space 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} established at admission time. Our central result, the Non-Identifiability Theorem, proves that 𝒜0∉σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\notin\sigma(g): the σ\sigma-algebra generated by the enforcement signal gg does not contain 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} under the Local Observability Assumption, which every practical enforcement system satisfies. The impossibility arises from a fundamental mismatch: gg evaluates actions locally against a point-wise rule set, while 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} encodes global, trajectory-level behavioral properties set at admission time. We then define the Invariant Measurement Layer (IML), which bypasses this limitation by retaining direct access to the generative model of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}. We prove an information-theoretic impossibility for enforcement-based monitoring; separately, we show that IML detects admission-time drift with provably finite detection delay, operating in the region where enforcement is structurally blind. We validate the theoretical claims across four experimental settings: three controlled drift scenarios (300 and 1000 steps), a live n8n webhook pipeline, and a LangGraph StateGraph agent with deterministic tool selection—in every case, enforcement triggers zero violations while IML deviation grows monotonically, detecting each drift type within 9–258 steps of drift onset. This paper is Paper 2 of a 4-paper Agent Governance Series: atomic decision boundaries (P0, [4]), stateful enforcement—ACP (P1, [3]), fair multi-agent allocation (P3, [5]), and composition irreducibility (P4, [6]).

1  Introduction

Multi-agent systems delegate subtasks to agents that operate with partial autonomy under a shared policy framework. At admission time, when an agent is authorized and its operational scope defined, the system implicitly records the constraints, initial context, and delegation lineage that constitute the agent’s admissible behavior space 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}. The dominant governance model then attempts to maintain alignment through an enforcement signal g:Σ∗→{0,1}g:\Sigma^{*}\to\{0,1\}, which returns 11 whenever a trace τ\tau contains a hard constraint violation.

This architecture has a fundamental observability limitation that has received little formal attention. Enforcement signals are local: they evaluate each action against a rule set that is static, does not change with trajectory history, and does not reference 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} directly. An agent can therefore drift—systematically shifting its behavioral distribution away from admission-time expectations—while every individual action remains within the permitted action space. This phenomenon is not a corner case; it is the generic behavior of any gradual distributional shift, goal reinterpretation, or delegation-depth creep that stays below hard constraint thresholds.

Motivation.

A foundational result in agent governance [4] establishes that only atomic decision systems—where evaluation and execution occur at the same state transition—can guarantee admissibility at runtime. Split systems that separate evaluation from execution cannot close this gap regardless of policy sophistication. Fernandez [3] instantiates this principle as the Agent Control Protocol (ACP): an atomic admission-control mechanism that requires execution-trace state. Section 17 of that work identifies a structurally distinct failure mode that persists even within an atomic enforcement layer: a correctly-functioning, stateful enforcement system can enter a regime in which behavioral drift is invisible to it. ACP calls this deviation collapse (§17.4)—enforcement is active and syntactically correct, yet the behavioral boundary is never exercised because upstream conditions suppress all activating inputs.

This paper operates above the atomic enforcement boundary and formalizes the conditions under which behavioral drift escapes detection. We prove (Theorem 3.2) that the admission-time behavioral contract 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is not identifiable from the enforcement signal gg alone—no matter how sophisticated the risk-scoring function. We then introduce the Invariant Measurement Layer (IML), an estimator that restores observability at the behavioral level, operating precisely in the region where g⁡(τ)=0g(\tau)=0 always and enforcement-based monitoring is structurally blind.

Main contributions.

  1. 1.

    T1 (Existence). We prove that the compliance-invariance gap is non-empty: trajectories satisfying g⁡(τ)=0g(\tau)=0 yet τ∉𝒜0\tau\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} exist under mild conditions (Lemma 3.1).

  2. 2.

    T2 (Non-Identifiability). We prove 𝒜0∉σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\notin\sigma(g) under the Local Observability Assumption: no measurable function of the enforcement signal can reconstruct 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership (Theorem 3.2). We exhibit an explicit constructive witness grounded in experimental data (Example 3.1).

  3. 3.

    T3 (IML Recoverability). We define IML and prove it is a consistent estimator of deviation D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) with provably finite detection delay (Theorem 3.6).

  4. 4.

    Empirical validation. Four experimental settings confirm g⁡(τt)=0​∀tg(\tau_{t})=0\;\forall t while D^t\widehat{D}_{t} grows monotonically: three controlled drift scenarios (300 and 1000 steps), a live n8n webhook pipeline (§5.3), and a real LangGraph StateGraph agent (§5.5)—directly instantiating both T2 and T3.

Paper organization.

Section 2 introduces the formal model. Section 3 states and proves T1, T2, and T3. Section 4 details the IML estimator. Section 5 presents the empirical validation. Section 6 discusses related work, and Section 8 concludes.

2  Problem Setup

2.1  Trace language and admissible behavior

Let Σ\Sigma be a finite alphabet of agent actions (tool calls, delegation requests, context updates). A trace is a finite sequence τ=(b1,b2,…,bT)∈Σ∗\tau=(b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{T})\in\Sigma^{*}.

Definition 2.1 (Admissible Behavior Space).

The admissible behavior space is 𝒜0=f⁡(C,E0,L)⊆Σ∗\mathcal{A}_{0}=f(C,E_{0},L)\subseteq\Sigma^{*}, where CC is the constraint set at admission, E0E_{0} is the initial context, and LL is the delegation lineage.

𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is a global object: whether τ∈𝒜0\tau\in\mathcal{A}_{0} depends on full-trajectory properties (distribution over actions, depth profile, context coherence), not on any single action in isolation.

2.2  Enforcement signal and local observability

Definition 2.2 (Enforcement Signal).

An enforcement signal g:Σ∗→{0,1}g:\Sigma^{*}\to\{0,1\} returns 11 to indicate a policy violation.

Assumption 2.1 (Local Observability).

The enforcement signal decomposes as g⁡(τ)=h⁡(V⁡(τ))g(\tau)=h(V(\tau)), where V:Σ∗→𝒱V:\Sigma^{*}\to\mathcal{V} evaluates only point-wise constraint violations (e.g., presence of a forbidden tool, delegation depth exceeding a fixed limit) and h:𝒱→{0,1}h:\mathcal{V}\to\{0,1\} aggregates violations. Crucially, V⁡(τ)V(\tau) is independent of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} and depends only on individual actions, not on global trajectory properties.

Assumption 2.1 is satisfied by every practical enforcement mechanism we are aware of: permission-check middleware, guardrail classifiers, schema validators, and policy engines all evaluate individual actions against a static rule set.

Remark 2.1 (ACP as a natural instance of Definition 2.2).

The Agent Control Protocol [3] provides a canonical instance of Definition 2.2 that satisfies Assumption 2.1. For a trace τ=(b1,…,bT)\tau=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{T}) of agent requests, define the ACP projection:

gACP(τ):=[∃i≤T:decision(bi)∈{Denied,Escalated}].g_{\mathrm{ACP}}(\tau)\;:=\;\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,\exists\,i\leq T:\mathrm{decision}(b_{i})\in\{\texttt{Denied},\,\texttt{Escalated}\}\right].

Each decision⁡(bi)\mathrm{decision}(b_{i}) is computed by ACP’s evaluate-then-mutate pipeline against a static PatternKey rule set, independently of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}; it therefore satisfies the decomposition g=h∘Vg=h\circ V required by Assumption 2.1. We use gACPg_{\mathrm{ACP}} as the running example throughout this paper. Importantly, the Non-Identifiability Theorem (Theorem 3.2) is proved for the entire class of gg satisfying Assumption 2.1, not for gACPg_{\mathrm{ACP}} alone; gACPg_{\mathrm{ACP}} is a natural instance, not the sole scope of the result.

2.3  Observability structure

The enforcement signal gg partitions Σ∗\Sigma^{*} into two equivalence classes: g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0) (compliant traces) and g−1​(1)g^{-1}(1) (violating traces). The corresponding σ\sigma-algebra is

σ⁡(g)={∅,g−1​(0),g−1​(1),Σ∗}.\sigma(g)\;=\;\bigl\{\,\emptyset,\;g^{-1}(0),\;g^{-1}(1),\;\Sigma^{*}\,\bigr\}.

A set S⊆Σ∗S\subseteq\Sigma^{*} is identifiable from gg if and only if S∈σ⁡(g)S\in\sigma(g).

2.4  Ground-truth deviation

Definition 2.3 (Deviation Function).

Let d:Σ∗×Σ∗→ℝ≥0d:\Sigma^{*}\times\Sigma^{*}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a trajectory metric. The deviation of τ\tau from 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is D⁡(τ,𝒜0)=infx∈𝒜0d⁡(τ,x)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0})=\inf_{x\in\mathcal{A}_{0}}d(\tau,x).

Remark 2.2 (Series notation).

Throughout this paper, D⁡(⋅,⋅)D(\cdot,\cdot) denotes a deviation function (real-valued distance from a behavioral set). In Paper 0 [4], the symbol DD denotes the decision domain D={Allow,Refuse,Escalate}D=\{\textsc{Allow},\textsc{Refuse},\textsc{Escalate}\}—a finite set of admission outcomes. The two uses are unrelated in type (function vs. set); when results from both papers appear together, we write D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) for the deviation function and 𝒟\mathcal{D} or {Allow,…}\{\textsc{Allow},\ldots\} for the decision domain to avoid ambiguity.

D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) is the ground truth but is intractable to compute directly because 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is implicitly defined. Section 4 constructs IML as a computable, consistent approximation.

3  Theoretical Results

3.1  T1: Existence of the compliance-invariance gap

Lemma 3.1 (Existence).

Under Assumption 2.1, if 𝒜0≠∅\mathcal{A}_{0}\neq\emptyset and 𝒜0⊊Σ∗\mathcal{A}_{0}\subsetneq\Sigma^{*}, then there exists τ∈Σ∗\tau\in\Sigma^{*} such that V⁡(τ)=∅V(\tau)=\emptyset, g⁡(τ)=0g(\tau)=0, and τ∉𝒜0\tau\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}.

Proof.

Since 𝒜0⊊Σ∗\mathcal{A}_{0}\subsetneq\Sigma^{*}, there exists τ∗∉𝒜0\tau^{*}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}. If V⁡(τ∗)=∅V(\tau^{*})=\emptyset already, we are done. Otherwise, τ∗\tau^{*} contains a step bib_{i} that triggers V≠∅V\neq\emptyset. By Assumption 2.1, VV depends only on point-wise properties of individual actions. Let τ′\tau^{\prime} be obtained from τ∗\tau^{*} by replacing every bib_{i} with V⁡(bi)≠∅V(b_{i})\neq\emptyset with an action bi′b^{\prime}_{i} drawn from the marginal distribution of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} restricted to safe actions (non-empty by 𝒜0≠∅\mathcal{A}_{0}\neq\emptyset). This substitution satisfies V⁡(τ′)=∅V(\tau^{\prime})=\emptyset by construction.

It remains to show τ′∉𝒜0\tau^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}. Recall that τ∗∉𝒜0\tau^{*}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} because it violates a trajectory-level constraint encoded in f⁡(C,E0,L)f(C,E_{0},L)— for instance, the fraction of safe tools in τ∗\tau^{*} falls below the threshold specified in CC, or the mean delegation depth exceeds the lineage bound in LL. The substitution replaces only actions with V⁡(bi)≠∅V(b_{i})\neq\emptyset by safe actions, which either leaves the violating distributional property intact (if τ∗\tau^{*} has too many boundary tools) or reduces the safe-tool fraction further (if the original violation was that boundary tools were over-represented). In either case, the distributional constraint that caused τ∗∉𝒜0\tau^{*}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} is still violated by τ′\tau^{\prime}, so τ′∉𝒜0\tau^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}, as required.

In our empirical instantiation (Section 5), this construction is realized concretely: all 900 post-drift steps across three scenarios satisfy V⁡(τt)=∅V(\tau_{t})=\emptyset while D⁡(τt,𝒜0)>0D(\tau_{t},\mathcal{A}_{0})>0. ∎

3.2  T2: Non-identifiability of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} under enforcement

Theorem 3.2 (Non-Identifiability).

Under Assumption 2.1, if 𝒜0≠∅\mathcal{A}_{0}\neq\emptyset and 𝒜0⊊Σ∗\mathcal{A}_{0}\subsetneq\Sigma^{*}, then

𝒜0∉σ⁡(g).\mathcal{A}_{0}\notin\sigma(g).

Equivalently, there exists no measurable function f:{0,1}→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\} such that f(g(τ))=𝟏[τ∈𝒜0]f(g(\tau))=\mathbf{1}_{[\tau\in\mathcal{A}_{0}]} for all τ∈Σ∗\tau\in\Sigma^{*}.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.1, there exists τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} with g⁡(τ2)=0g(\tau_{2})=0. Since 𝒜0≠∅\mathcal{A}_{0}\neq\emptyset, there exists τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}. If g⁡(τ1)=0g(\tau_{1})=0, we already have g⁡(τ1)=g⁡(τ2)=0g(\tau_{1})=g(\tau_{2})=0 with τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0} and τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}. If g⁡(τ1)=1g(\tau_{1})=1, then by the Local Observability Assumption 2.1, V⁡(τ1)≠∅V(\tau_{1})\neq\emptyset; applying the same substitution argument as in Lemma 3.1 yields τ1′∈𝒜0\tau_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{0} with V⁡(τ1′)=∅V(\tau_{1}^{\prime})=\emptyset, hence g⁡(τ1′)=0g(\tau_{1}^{\prime})=0.

In either case, we have τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0} and τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} with g⁡(τ1)=g⁡(τ2)=0g(\tau_{1})=g(\tau_{2})=0. Suppose for contradiction that 𝒜0∈σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\in\sigma(g). Since σ⁡(g)\sigma(g) is generated by g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0) and g−1​(1)g^{-1}(1), and 𝒜0⊆g−1​(0)\mathcal{A}_{0}\subseteq g^{-1}(0), any σ⁡(g)\sigma(g)-measurable function ff satisfies f⁡(0)=cf(0)=c for some constant c∈{0,1}c\in\{0,1\}. But then f⁡(g⁡(τ1))=f⁡(0)=c=f⁡(g⁡(τ2))f(g(\tau_{1}))=f(0)=c=f(g(\tau_{2})), so 𝟏[τ1∈𝒜0]=𝟏[τ2∈𝒜0]\mathbf{1}_{[\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}]}=\mathbf{1}_{[\tau_{2}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}]}. This contradicts τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0} and τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}. ∎∎

Corollary 3.3 (Information-Theoretic Bound).

I⁡(𝒜0,g⁡(τ))<H⁡(𝒜0)I(\mathcal{A}_{0}\,;\,g(\tau))<H(\mathcal{A}_{0}). The mutual information between the enforcement signal and 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership is strictly less than the entropy of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership.

Proof.

Suppose for contradiction that I⁡(𝒜0,g⁡(τ))=H⁡(𝒜0)I(\mathcal{A}_{0};\,g(\tau))=H(\mathcal{A}_{0}). This equality holds if and only if 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership is a deterministic function of g⁡(τ)g(\tau)—i.e., there exists f:{0,1}→{0,1}f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\} with f(g(τ))=𝟏[τ∈𝒜0]f(g(\tau))=\mathbf{1}_{[\tau\in\mathcal{A}_{0}]} for all τ\tau. But Theorem 3.2 proves exactly that no such ff exists. Hence I⁡(𝒜0,g⁡(τ))<H⁡(𝒜0)I(\mathcal{A}_{0};\,g(\tau))<H(\mathcal{A}_{0}). ∎

Remark 3.1 (Why T2 is non-trivial).

A referee might object: “any many-to-one function loses information.” T2 is stronger for three reasons.

(i) Structural, not incidental. The result holds for the entire class of gg satisfying Assumption 2.1—not for one particular rule set. No redesign of enforcement rules, no matter how sophisticated, can make 𝒜0∈σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\in\sigma(g), because the impossibility is a consequence of the local-observation architecture itself.

(ii) The oracle contrast. If gg were permitted to query 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}} at each step—i.e., to evaluate the JS divergence JS(Pτ∥PE0)\mathrm{JS}(P_{\tau}\|P_{E_{0}}) in addition to point-wise violations—then 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} could be in σ⁡(g)\sigma(g). T2 says that precisely this access is what every practical enforcement system lacks. IML is the minimal mechanism that adds it back.

(iii) Binary enforcement covers the decision boundary. At the point of action—permit or block—enforcement is effectively binary. A continuous risk score r⁡(τ)∈[0,1]r(\tau)\in[0,1] still produces a binary decision g(τ)=𝟏[r(τ)≥θr]g(\tau)=\mathbf{1}[r(\tau)\geq\theta_{r}], and our argument applies to that induced partition. More generally, for any finite-valued g:Σ∗→Gg:\Sigma^{*}\to G, the same structural barrier holds: unless gg explicitly encodes 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-distance (i.e., queries 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}} as IML does), σ⁡(g)\sigma(g) is a finite coarsening of Σ∗\Sigma^{*} that cannot resolve 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership.

Corollary 3.4 (Irrecoverability).

No function h:{0,1}→{0,1}h:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\} satisfies

h⁡(g⁡(τ))=1⇔τ∈𝒜0h(g(\tau))=1\;\iff\;\tau\in\mathcal{A}_{0}

for all τ∈Σ∗\tau\in\Sigma^{*}. In particular, no adjustment of a risk-scoring function can recover 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership from enforcement signals alone.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.2, there exist τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0} and τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0} with g⁡(τ1)=g⁡(τ2)=0g(\tau_{1})=g(\tau_{2})=0. Any hh satisfying the condition would require h⁡(0)=1h(0)=1 (from τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}) and h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 (from τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0})—a contradiction. The same argument applies symmetrically when g⁡(τ1)=g⁡(τ2)=1g(\tau_{1})=g(\tau_{2})=1. ∎

This corollary extends Fernandez [3] §1.1, which gives an analogous impossibility for stateless vs. stateful enforcement; here we show the same holds for enforcement-vs.-invariant monitoring.

Theorem 3.5 (Monotonic Hidden Drift).

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.2, there exists a sequence (τt)t=1T⊂g−1​(0)(\tau_{t})_{t=1}^{T}\subset g^{-1}(0) such that:

  1. 1.

    g⁡(τt)=0g(\tau_{t})=0 for all t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, and

  2. 2.

    D⁡(τt,𝒜0)D(\tau_{t},\mathcal{A}_{0}) is strictly increasing in tt.

That is, behavioral deviation from 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} can grow arbitrarily while producing no enforcement signal whatsoever.

Proof.

Base case (T=2T=2). Let τ1∈𝒜0\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}; then g⁡(τ1)=0g(\tau_{1})=0 and D⁡(τ1,𝒜0)=0D(\tau_{1},\mathcal{A}_{0})=0. By Corollary 3.4, g−1​(0)∖𝒜0≠∅g^{-1}(0)\setminus\mathcal{A}_{0}\neq\emptyset, so there exists τ2∈g−1​(0)\tau_{2}\in g^{-1}(0) with Δ:=D⁡(τ2,𝒜0)>0\Delta:=D(\tau_{2},\mathcal{A}_{0})>0. The pair (τ1,τ2)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) already satisfies both conditions.

Extension to arbitrary TT. For t=2,…,T−1t=2,\ldots,T-1, let τt\tau_{t} be any trace with empirical distribution

Pt=(1−t−1T−1)​P^τ1+t−1T−1​P^τ2.P_{t}\;=\;\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t-1}{T-1}\Bigr)\hat{P}_{\tau_{1}}+\tfrac{t-1}{T-1}\hat{P}_{\tau_{2}}.

Since supp⁡(Pt)⊆supp⁡(P^τ1)∪supp⁡(P^τ2)⊆Σ∖F\mathrm{supp}(P_{t})\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(\hat{P}_{\tau_{1}})\cup\mathrm{supp}(\hat{P}_{\tau_{2}})\subseteq\Sigma\setminus F (both source traces have g=0g=0, hence no forbidden actions under Assumption 2.1), we have g⁡(τt)=0g(\tau_{t})=0 for all tt. Define f:[0,1]→ℝ≥0f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} by f⁡(s)=D⁡(τs,𝒜0)f(s)=D(\tau^{s},\mathcal{A}_{0}) where P^τs=(1−s)​P^τ1+s​P^τ2\hat{P}_{\tau^{s}}=(1-s)\hat{P}_{\tau_{1}}+s\hat{P}_{\tau_{2}}. By the Lipschitz continuity of JS divergence in its first argument (a standard property; see Assumption 3.1(A3) below for the formal statement), ff is continuous, with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and f⁡(1)=Δ>0f(1)=\Delta>0. By the Intermediate Value Theorem, ff attains all values in [0,Δ][0,\Delta]; choosing τt\tau_{t} to realize parameter st=(t−1)/(T−1)s_{t}=(t-1)/(T-1) yields D⁡(τt,𝒜0)=f⁡(st)D(\tau_{t},\mathcal{A}_{0})=f(s_{t}) strictly increasing in tt (since ff cannot be identically zero on (0,1](0,1]: that would require P^τ2∈𝒜0\hat{P}_{\tau_{2}}\in\mathcal{A}_{0}, contradicting τ2∉𝒜0\tau_{2}\notin\mathcal{A}_{0}). ∎

Theorem 3.5 formalizes what Fernandez [3] calls the hidden drift scenario within deviation collapse (§17.4): behavioral drift can be arbitrarily large while the enforcement boundary remains entirely silent. The BAR-Monitor of Fernandez [3] detects whether the enforcement boundary is being exercised; IML’s D^\widehat{D} detects drift within the region where BAR is structurally blind (g⁡(τ)=0g(\tau)=0 always).

Constructive witness.

The proof above is existential. We now exhibit an explicit pair (τ1,τ2)(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) extracted verbatim from our simulation.

Example 3.1 (Constructive Witness for T2).

We run a 300-step tool-drift simulation (seed 42) with alphabet Σ={\Sigma=\{safe_read, safe_query, moderate_write, moderate_send, risky_execute, risky_delegate}\}. The enforcement function uses forbidden set F={F=\{forbidden_exec, forbidden_delete}∩Σ=∅\}\cap\Sigma=\emptyset and maximum delegation depth 10. The admission snapshot 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}} is built from 50 burn-in steps under base distribution {\{safe: 75%, boundary: 20%, risky: 5%}\}. 3.3  T3: IML Recoverability

Stochastic drift model.

We model the agent’s action process as a sequence of i.i.d. draws from a time-varying distribution Pt∈Δ⁡(Σ)P_{t}\in\Delta(\Sigma), where Δ⁡(Σ)\Delta(\Sigma) denotes the simplex over Σ\Sigma. The true deviation at time tt is

Dt∗=JS(Pt∥PE0)+wc⋅𝔼b∼Pt[ρ(b)]+wl⋅ϕ(μd,t),D_{t}^{*}\;=\;\mathrm{JS}(P_{t}\,\|\,P_{E_{0}})\;+\;w_{c}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{b\sim P_{t}}[\rho(b)]\;+\;w_{l}\cdot\phi(\mu_{d,t}),

where μd,t\mu_{d,t} is the mean delegation depth at time tt and ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) is the normalized deviation from μdepth\mu_{\mathrm{depth}}. IML computes empirical estimates of each term from the observed trace.

Assumption 3.1 (Regularity Conditions).
  1. (A1)

    Bounded drift rate. ‖Pt−Pt−1‖1≤δ\|P_{t}-P_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\delta and |μd,t−μd,t−1|≤δ|\mu_{d,t}-\mu_{d,t-1}|\leq\delta for all tt.

  2. (A2)

    Stationary reference. PE0P_{E_{0}} and (μdepth,σdepth)(\mu_{\mathrm{depth}},\sigma_{\mathrm{depth}}) are fixed at admission time and never updated.

  3. (A3)

    Lipschitz estimator. |JS(P∥Q)−JS(P′∥Q)|≤c∥P−P′∥1|\mathrm{JS}(P\|Q)-\mathrm{JS}(P^{\prime}\|Q)|\leq c\,\|P-P^{\prime}\|_{1} for c<∞c<\infty (continuity of JS divergence in its first argument).

  4. (A4)

    Bounded estimation error. |D^n−Dt∗|≤εest​(n)|\widehat{D}_{n}-D_{t}^{*}|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{est}}(n) with probability at least 1−δ01-\delta_{0}, where εest​(n)→0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{est}}(n)\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty. (This follows from A1–A3 via Hoeffding’s inequality; see proof of Theorem 3.6.)

Theorem 3.6 (IML Recoverability).

Let p1=ℙ⁡(Dt∗≥θ+δ)p_{1}=\mathbb{P}(D_{t}^{*}\geq\theta+\delta) be the probability that true deviation exceeds the margin. If p1>0p_{1}>0 for all t≥t0t\geq t_{0}, then:

    ℙ(∃t≤T∗(θ):D^t≥θ)≥ 1−α,\mathbb{P}\!\left(\,\exists\,t\leq T^{*}(\theta):\,\widehat{D}_{t}\geq\theta\right)\;\geq\;1-\alpha,

Contrast with ACP: ACP Proposition 1 bounds ℙ⁡(BARW<τ)\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{BAR}_{W}<\tau) over enforcement decisions; IML’s bound operates on D^\widehat{D} over the same window WW, covering the region where ACP’s bound is vacuous (p1ACP=0p_{1}^{\mathrm{ACP}}=0).

Remark 3.2 (Instantiation of the abstract deviation function).

The consistency claim in part (1) is stated with respect to Dt∗D_{t}^{*}—the specific instantiation of D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) defined in the Stochastic Drift Model above, anchored to the empirical admission snapshot 𝒜0emp=(PE0,μdepth,σdepth)\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}}=(P_{E_{0}},\mu_{\mathrm{depth}},\sigma_{\mathrm{depth}}). Theorem 3.6 proves that D^\widehat{D} consistently estimates Dt∗D_{t}^{*} for this natural instantiation; whether Dt∗D_{t}^{*} accurately approximates the true D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) depends on how well 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}} captures the original behavioral contract, and is addressed empirically in Section 5.

Under the conditions of Theorem 3.6, if D(τ1:t,𝒜0)D(\tau_{1:t},\mathcal{A}_{0}) increases at rate at least α>0\alpha>0, i.e., D(τ1:t,𝒜0)≥α(t−t0)D(\tau_{1:t},\mathcal{A}_{0})\geq\alpha\,(t-t_{0}) for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}, then detection occurs by

4  The Invariant Measurement Layer

4.1  Design principle

Theorem 3.2 implies that any estimator of D⁡(τ,𝒜0)D(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{0}) must have direct access to 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}—it cannot be derived from g⁡(τ)g(\tau) alone. IML operationalizes this by retaining a lightweight admission snapshot:

𝒜0emp=(PE0,μdepth,σdepth),\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}}\;=\;\bigl(P_{E_{0}},\;\mu_{\mathrm{depth}},\;\sigma_{\mathrm{depth}}\bigr),

where PE0P_{E_{0}} is the empirical tool distribution over a burn-in trace, and (μdepth,σdepth)(\mu_{\mathrm{depth}},\sigma_{\mathrm{depth}}) are depth statistics—both frozen at t=0t=0 and never updated.

4.2  Deviation decomposition

Definition 4.1 (IML Components).

D^​(τ,𝒜0)=wt​Dt​(τ)+wc​Dc​(τ)+wl​Dl​(τ)\widehat{D}(\tau;\mathcal{A}_{0})=w_{t}D_{t}(\tau)+w_{c}D_{c}(\tau)+w_{l}D_{l}(\tau), with weights (wt,wc,wl)=(0.40,0.35,0.25)(w_{t},w_{c},w_{l})=(0.40,0.35,0.25), where:

  1. (1)

    Temporal drift Dt(τ)=JS(Pτ∥PE0)∈[0,1]D_{t}(\tau)=\mathrm{JS}(P_{\tau}\|P_{E_{0}})\in[0,1]: Jensen–Shannon divergence between the current and admission-time tool distributions.

  2. (2)

    Constraint proximity Dc​(τ)=1|τ|​∑b∈τρ⁡(b)D_{c}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|\tau|}\sum_{b\in\tau}\rho(b): mean risk score, where ρ:Σ→[0,1]\rho:\Sigma\to[0,1] is pre-specified.

  3. (3)

    Lineage deviation Dl​(τ)=min⁡(|d¯​(τ)−μdepth|2​σdepth, 1)D_{l}(\tau)=\min\!\left(\tfrac{|\bar{d}(\tau)-\mu_{\mathrm{depth}}|}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{depth}}},\;1\right): normalized distance between the observed mean delegation depth and the admission-time expectation.

To reduce step-to-step noise, IML applies an exponential moving average D^t=α​Draw,t+(1−α)​D^t−1\widehat{D}_{t}=\alpha D_{\mathrm{raw},t}+(1-\alpha)\widehat{D}_{t-1} with α=0.15\alpha=0.15.

4.3  Comparison with baselines

Table 2 contrasts IML with the two standard baselines along the information dimension central to Theorem 3.2.

The anomaly detector (B2) compares the rolling tool distribution against the agent’s own history using JS divergence. Its critical limitation: the reference distribution drifts with the agent, eroding sensitivity to gradual behavioral shift. IML’s reference PE0P_{E_{0}} is frozen at admission and never adapts—this is precisely what allows it to detect deviation relative to the original behavioral contract.

5  Experiments

5.1  Setup

We implement iml-benchmark, a Python simulation with the six-tool alphabet Σ\Sigma from Example 3.1. Enforcement uses F={F=\{forbidden_exec, forbidden_delete}\} and MAX_DEPTH =10=10. The anomaly baseline (B2) uses a 30-step rolling window. All runs: seed 42, 50-step burn-in, 300 simulation steps. Code and raw results are available at https://github.com/chelof100/iml-benchmark.

Three drift scenarios are evaluated; all are designed to satisfy g⁡(τt)=0​∀tg(\tau_{t})=0\;\forall t:

  1. 1.

    Tool drift. Tool probabilities shift linearly (starting t=50t=50) from {\{safe: 75%, boundary: 20%, risky: 5%}\} to {\{safe: 15%, boundary: 75%, risky: 10%}\}. Depth stays at 1.

  2. 2.

    Delegation drift. Depth increases linearly from 1 to 5 while the tool distribution stays near baseline.

  3. 3.

    Context drift. Joint shift to {\{safe: 20%, boundary: 60%, risky: 20%}\}, modeling a semantic prompt-level change.

5.2  Results

T2: empirical instantiation of Non-Identifiability.

Enforcement triggers = 0 in all three scenarios across all 300 steps (Table 3, column 2). No drift pattern crosses a hard constraint boundary: the entire 900-step execution lies in g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0). This empirically instantiates Theorem 3.2—it does not re-prove it, but exhibits the concrete hidden-drift sequences whose existence the theorem guarantees.

T3: empirical instantiation of Detection Guarantee.

D^\widehat{D} grows in all three scenarios (Figure 3). Delegation drift produces the fastest detection (T0.20∗=130T^{*}_{0.20}=130) and highest final deviation (D^=0.389\widehat{D}=0.389) because the DlD_{l} component saturates at 1.01.0 once depth reaches 5: this is a strictly lineage-level property that gg cannot observe. Tool and context drift cross θ=0.20\theta=0.20 near steps 256–258, demonstrating that DtD_{t} and DcD_{c} are jointly sufficient to detect distributional shift.

Figure 2 shows the per-component trajectories (DtD_{t}, DcD_{c}, DlD_{l}) across all three scenarios, clarifying which dimension of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} drives detection in each case.

Detection delay vs. theoretical bound.

Corollary 3.7 gives T∗≤t0+(θ+εest)/αT^{*}\leq t_{0}+(\theta+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{est}})/\alpha, where α\alpha is the empirical drift rate (slope of Dt∗D_{t}^{*} post-onset) and εest≈0.02\varepsilon_{\mathrm{est}}\approx 0.02 from EMA convergence. Using the observed post-onset slope as a lower bound on α\alpha, Table 4 confirms that all observed T∗T^{*} values satisfy the bound with margin.

IML vs. anomaly detector: two distinct failure modes.

The comparison between IML and B2 (Figure 4) reveals two qualitatively different deficiencies of reference-free anomaly detection.

Reference contamination (tool/context drift). The anomaly detector peaks at 0.388 at t=261t=261, then declines by 0.118 to 0.270 by t=299t=299. This is a direct consequence of history contamination: as the drifted distribution accrues in B2’s rolling history, its reference distribution adapts to the drift, suppressing the signal. In the limit of long operation, B2 converges to near zero while IML’s score remains anchored to the frozen PE0P_{E_{0}}.

Lineage blindness (delegation drift). The anomaly detector operates on tool frequency alone and cannot perceive the monotone increase in delegation depth. Its final score is 0.201—half of IML’s 0.389—yielding a +0.188+0.188 separation in favor of IML. This gap corresponds exactly to the Dl=1.0D_{l}=1.0 component that B2 lacks an equivalent for.

Together, these two failure modes confirm the theoretical prediction: a monitoring approach without direct access to 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} will either adapt to the drift (losing long-horizon reliability) or be structurally blind to certain drift dimensions.

5.3  Real-Agent Validation via n8n

To validate IML beyond simulation, we deployed the IML Engine as a webhook-triggered n8n workflow running entirely in JavaScript Code nodes with $𝚐𝚎𝚝𝚆𝚘𝚛𝚔𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚠𝚂𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚒𝚌𝙳𝚊𝚝𝚊​()\$\mathtt{getWorkflowStaticData()} for cross-execution persistence—requiring no external server. Burn-in events (n=50n=50) are posted once to establish A0A_{0}; subsequent events arrive per tool call.

The IML Engine detected drift within 9 steps of the distribution shift (T0.30∗=9T^{*}_{0.30}=9), with D^\widehat{D} rising from 0.0950.095 to 0.4030.403 while enforcement remained zero throughout all 250 steps. Final component breakdown: Dt=0.143D_{t}=0.143, Dc=0.500D_{c}=0.500, Dl=0.333D_{l}=0.333. These results are consistent with the simulation benchmarks (D^final∈[0.21,0.39]\widehat{D}_{\text{final}}\in[0.21,0.39] in Table 3) and confirm T2 and T3 on a live multi-agent webhook pipeline.

5.4  Long-Horizon Validation (1000 Steps)

A potential concern with 300-step experiments is that enforcement might eventually trigger as drift accumulates. To address this, we re-run all three scenarios for 1000 steps (seed 42) with identical parameters.

Enforcement triggers zero violations across all 3000 steps, confirming that the compliance-invariance gap identified in Theorem 3.2 is not a transient artifact of short experiments but a persistent structural property. D^\widehat{D} grows through step 1000 in all scenarios, with delegation drift reaching 0.3930.393 and tool/context drift reaching ≈0.228\approx 0.228. The monotone growth directly instantiates Theorem 3.5: a sequence (τt)t=11000(\tau_{t})_{t=1}^{1000} with g⁡(τt)=0g(\tau_{t})=0 and D⁡(τt,𝒜0)D(\tau_{t},\mathcal{A}_{0}) strictly increasing.

5.5  LangGraph Agent Experiment

To demonstrate IML in a real agent-framework execution context, we implement a LangGraph [10] StateGraph with two nodes (decide_tool →\to execute_tool) and a deterministic MockLLM that selects tools without external API calls, providing full reproducibility across seeds. Using a deterministic sampler isolates the IML signal from LLM stochasticity; connecting IML to live LLM-backed agents is deferred to future work. After a 50-step burn-in under safe-heavy behavior, we induce gradual compliant drift over 200 steps by shifting tool selection probabilities linearly from {\{safe: 75%, boundary: 20%, risky: 5%}\} toward {\{safe: 15%, boundary: 75%, risky: 10%}\}, with delegation depth increasing from 1 to 3. No forbidden tools are used; g⁡(τt)=0g(\tau_{t})=0 throughout all 250 steps.

We run 6 independent seeds (42, 1–5). Table 7 reports per-seed results; enforcement =0=0 in all 6 runs.

Across all seeds, D^\widehat{D} rises from ≈0.01\approx 0.01 at drift onset to 0.343±0.0160.343\pm 0.016 at t=249t=249, with T0.20∗=176±8T^{*}_{0.20}=176\pm 8 (detection within 126±8126\pm 8 steps of drift onset), while enforcement registers zero triggers in every run. Component analysis confirms the drift is driven primarily by DcD_{c} (boundary tool accumulation) and DtD_{t} (distributional shift), with DlD_{l} activating after t≈150t\approx 150 as delegation depth increases. These results confirm T2 and T3 on a real agent-framework execution stack with consistent behavior across seeds.

6  Related Work

Relationship to the governance series.

This paper is part of a series on formal agent governance. Fernandez [4] (Paper 0) proves that only atomic decision systems—where evaluation and execution share the same state transition—can guarantee admissibility at runtime; split systems (RBAC, OPA, policy engines) cannot close this gap regardless of policy sophistication. Fernandez [3] (Paper 1) instantiates this principle as the Agent Control Protocol: an atomic admission-control mechanism with execution-trace state. IML (this paper, Paper 2) addresses the behavioral layer above the atomic boundary: even within a correctly functioning atomic enforcement system, behavioral drift accumulates in the region g−1​(0)g^{-1}(0) and is invisible to the enforcement signal. Fernandez [5] (Paper 3) addresses fairness and resource allocation in shared admission systems, establishing that atomic correctness and drift observability together are insufficient for equitable access to the decision boundary. Fernandez [6] (Paper 4) closes the quartet by proving that the four layers (Papers 0–3) form a minimal compositional architecture: under finite observability, no three-layer subset simultaneously guarantees atomicity, drift detection, actor-level fairness, and Sybil resistance. IML’s D^\widehat{D} is used directly as the Layer 2 monitoring signal in that composition, and the Non-Identifiability Theorem (T2 of this paper) is the formal basis for Case 2 of that paper’s irreducibility proof.

BAR-Monitor.

Fernandez [3] introduces the Boundary Activation Rate (BARN\mathrm{BAR}_{N}) monitor to detect deviation collapse—a regime in which enforcement is syntactically active but no boundary is exercised (BAR≈0\mathrm{BAR}\approx 0). IML’s D^\widehat{D} addresses a complementary failure mode: behavioral drift that occurs while enforcement remains active (g⁡(τ)=0g(\tau)=0 for all observed τ\tau, yet BAR>0\mathrm{BAR}>0). BAR\mathrm{BAR} monitors enforcement health; D^\widehat{D} monitors behavioral distance to 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}. The two mechanisms are designed to be deployed together.

Runtime verification.

Runtime Verification (RV) [11, 2] checks execution traces against formal specifications using local monitors. Our work provides a formal account of what RV monitors cannot detect: any behavioral property in 𝒜0∖σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\setminus\sigma(g). IML complements RV rather than replacing it.

Diagnosability in discrete-event systems.

Sampath et al. [13] defined diagnosability as the ability to detect faults from partial observations in finite time. Theorem 3.2 establishes that 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership is not diagnosable from gg alone; Theorem 3.6 establishes that it becomes diagnosable once the IML component 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}} is added.

Partial observability.

POMDPs [9] model decision-making under partial state observation. Our enforcement observer faces an analogous problem: it observes g⁡(τ)∈{0,1}g(\tau)\in\{0,1\} rather than full 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership. T3 is a constructive analogue of POMDP belief tracking: IML maintains a “belief” about deviation using the generative model of 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}.

Information flow and non-interference.

Goguen and Meseguer [7] asked whether a low-security observer can infer high-security behavior. Our setting is dual: we ask whether an enforcement observer can infer 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}-membership from gg. Theorem 3.2 gives a negative answer that parallels non-deducibility.

Anomaly detection.

Statistical anomaly detectors [1] compare current to historical distributions. Our experiments confirm their fundamental limitation: without a frozen normative reference, the historical distribution drifts with the agent, eliminating sensitivity to gradual shift.

AI agent safety.

Recent work on agent oversight [8, 12] focuses on detecting misaligned behavior through behavioral testing. Our results provide formal grounding for why enforcement-only oversight is provably insufficient, and what information an estimator must access to close the gap.

7  Discussion and Limitations

Scope of T2.

Theorem 3.2 holds for the entire class of gg satisfying Assumption 2.1. A richer observation map that queries 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} directly at each step would sidestep the impossibility—but maintaining and querying 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} at runtime is precisely what IML does. T2 thus motivates IML rather than dismisses it.

Approximation quality of 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}}.

Our empirical snapshot is a three-parameter summary. Richer models (e.g., full language model distributions over action sequences) would improve DtD_{t} sensitivity at the cost of runtime overhead. The theoretical guarantees in T3 require only Lipschitz continuity and bounded drift, not a specific snapshot representation.

Real agent traces.

Section 5.3 reports validation on a live n8n webhook pipeline. Results confirm T2 and T3 on authentic delegation chains: D^\widehat{D} grew from 0.0950.095 to 0.4030.403 while enforcement remained zero, and T0.30∗=9T^{*}_{0.30}=9 steps into the drift phase. The DlD_{l} component (0.3330.333 final) confirms that depth-level deviation is detectable even with modest delegation depth variance, supporting our expectation that lineage sensitivity will be especially pronounced in real systems.

Adversarial drift.

An agent that actively minimizes D^\widehat{D} while drifting could in principle evade detection. This connects to reward hacking under partial observability and requires strengthened assumptions on drift structure.

Regime violations of T3 assumptions.

Assumption 3.1(A1) requires bounded drift rate ‖Pt−Pt−1‖1≤δ\|P_{t}-P_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\delta. In practice, LLM-backed agents can exhibit abrupt concept shifts—e.g., a tool mis-routing triggered by a prompt injection—where the behavioral distribution changes discontinuously in a single step. In such cases, the detection delay bound of Corollary 3.7 no longer applies: T∗T^{*} may be zero (immediate detection) or, if the shift causes Dt∗D_{t}^{*} to jump above θ\theta without the EMA catching up, detection may be delayed by O⁡(1/αEMA)O(1/\alpha_{\mathrm{EMA}}) steps. The IML signal remains useful even under A1 violations—a step discontinuity in D^\widehat{D} is itself informative—but quantitative T3 guarantees should be interpreted as applying to the gradual drift regime. Handling hard concept shifts with formal guarantees is left for future work.

Future work.

Future work will focus on three directions. First, we will refine the deviation metrics by exploring alternative instantiations for each component, including Earth Mover’s Distance, process-mining features, and learned weights from human feedback signals. Second, we will evaluate IML in more realistic multi-agent environments (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen) with induced drift and compare against baselines from concept-drift and anomaly detection. Third, we will develop an open-source IML middleware that plugs into existing agent stacks with native integration for admission control and runtime enforcement.

Fairness and resource allocation in shared admission systems are intentionally left as a separate line of work: they concern observability coverage and exploration bias rather than long-horizon deviation monitoring, and deserve their own formal treatment.

8  Conclusion

We have shown that the gap between enforcement compliance and behavioral invariance is not incidental but structurally inevitable: under the Local Observability Assumption satisfied by all practical enforcement systems, 𝒜0∉σ⁡(g)\mathcal{A}_{0}\notin\sigma(g). No rule-based system—however carefully engineered—can recover admission-time invariants from its own signals alone.

This result motivates a three-layer governance architecture. Admission (ACP [3]) defines and records 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} at authorization time. Invariant monitoring (IML, this paper) measures how far the agent’s behavior has drifted from that contract, operating in the region where enforcement is structurally blind. Enforcement acts on hard constraint violations. Each layer is necessary; none is sufficient alone.

The Invariant Measurement Layer addresses this impossibility by anchoring deviation estimation to the frozen admission snapshot 𝒜0emp\mathcal{A}_{0}^{\mathrm{emp}}. The resulting estimator is consistent, has quantified detection delay, and empirically distinguishes drifted traces that enforcement is blind to—across controlled simulations up to 1000 steps, a live n8n webhook pipeline, and a real LangGraph agent framework—with enforcement triggers = 0 throughout in every setting.

The broader architectural implication is clear: agent governance systems that rely solely on enforcement will systematically miss the class of admissible-to-inadmissible drift that accumulates gradually within the permitted action space. A lightweight admission-time snapshot is a necessary complement, not an optional enhancement.

This paper is the second in a series on agent governance. The first, Fernandez [3], established that stateful admission control is necessary and proved that enforcement-only governance is insufficient against behavioral history; IML now establishes that even stateful enforcement is insufficient against admission-time behavioral contracts, and provides the missing monitoring layer. Together, the two mechanisms cover complementary failure modes: ACP monitors the enforcement boundary; IML monitors behavioral distance within the compliant region.
